planting.note: Plant dormant, bare-root bushes in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained soil; Houghton is one of the oldest American gooseberry selections and tolerates summer heat better than most European cultivars.

directions: Houghton is one of the oldest American gooseberry cultivars, raised from seed at Lynn, Massachusetts in 1833 and kept in cultivation for generations as an easy, reliable dooryard bush with notably better tolerance of summer heat and powdery mildew than most English dessert types. The spreading, moderately thorny bush bears abundant small to medium pale greenish-pink berries with a mild, sweet-tart flavor suited to fresh eating as well as pies and preserves. It is self-fertile and needs no companion planting, which makes it a forgiving choice for a first gooseberry bush. Prune out the oldest canes each winter and keep the center of the bush open to encourage airflow and limit mildew in humid climates.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool, fertile, well-drained soil; Crown Bob is a very old English red dessert gooseberry still grown by heritage fruit specialists.

directions: Crown Bob is a very old English red dessert gooseberry, grown since the early nineteenth century and long prized at gooseberry club shows for its large, hairy, deep red fruit with a rich flavor once fully ripe. The vigorous, spreading bush crops heavily and adapts to a range of soils provided drainage is good, though like other European gooseberries it benefits from cool root conditions and a watchful eye for mildew. Pick fruit slightly underripe and firm for cooking, or let berries hang until soft and deeply colored for the best dessert flavor. Thin congested growth each winter to an open framework to improve air circulation and make harvesting easier among the thorns.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring; Warrington is a late-ripening English red gooseberry that holds well on the bush after other red cultivars have finished.

directions: Warrington is a classic late-season English red gooseberry, still one of the most widely available heritage cultivars for home orchards. Its hairy, dark red berries ripen later than most other red cultivars and hold well on the bush, developing a rich, sweet-tart dessert flavor, though they also work well in jams and pies if picked a little earlier. The upright, vigorous bush is a dependable cropper and shows reasonably good resistance to mildew for an older English cultivar. Prune in the dormant season to an open, goblet-shaped framework and mulch well, since Warrington performs best with cool, consistently moist root conditions.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring; Yellow Champagne is a historic English dessert gooseberry grown mainly by heirloom fruit collectors.

directions: Yellow Champagne is a historic English dessert gooseberry traced to the grounds of Duplin Castle, grown for its small, hairy, pale golden berries, which have a sweet, rich flavor for a gooseberry and are often eaten fresh rather than cooked, though it is generally considered milder than its sibling Red Champagne. The spreading bush is moderately vigorous and crops reliably once established, though yields tend to run lighter than modern large-fruited cultivars. It suits collectors of heirloom fruit and heritage orchards more than high-volume home production. Site in full sun to partial shade in cool, moist, fertile soil, and prune out old wood each winter to keep the thorny bush open and productive.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; Howard's Lancer is an English red dessert gooseberry bred for improved mildew resistance.

directions: Howard's Lancer, often sold simply as Lancer, is an English red dessert gooseberry bred as an improvement on older red cultivars, combining large fruit size with better resistance to American gooseberry mildew. The smooth-skinned, bright red berries ripen in midseason with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor suited to fresh eating as well as cooking. The upright bush is moderately vigorous and crops well once established, settling in within a couple of seasons. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune annually in the dormant season to an open framework to maximize light penetration and ease of harvest among the thorns.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in rich, well-drained soil; Dan's Mistake is a quirky-named heirloom English gooseberry rarely found outside specialist fruit nurseries.

directions: Dan's Mistake is a quirky-named heirloom English gooseberry, a rare variety stocked mainly by specialist fruit nurseries and long associated with the competitive gooseberry shows of northern England, where growers have exhibited giant-fruited cultivars for well over a century. Its large, pale green berries are grown chiefly for size and show rather than commercial sale, though they are perfectly good to eat fresh or cooked once fully ripe and softened. The spreading bush is vigorous and responds well to heavy feeding and fruit thinning if maximum berry size is the goal. Grow in rich, well-drained soil in a cool spot with some afternoon shade in warm climates, and prune to an open framework each winter to ease harvest among the thorns.
